title: CLO 2025 Academic Month: Sutured and Unsutured

summary: # CLO 2025 Academic Month: Sutured and Unsutured ## Introduction I'd like to introduce myself. My name is Catherine Andreuzzi. I'm a full-time professor in the apparel design department at the Rhode Island School of Design (RISD). We've put together a presentation that we also gave, Joy and I. Joy is with me; you'll meet her later. She is a faculty member in the textiles department at RISD. We gave this presentation at the New York CLO Summit last fall, and it was really well received, so we're very happy to do it again and to be asked. ## Presentation Overview We’re going to take you through what we’re calling "Stitched and Unstitched." Fittingly, I work with stitched materials, and Joy works with unstitched materials. I'm going to start the presentation with some of my apparel students' work. ### Student Projects: Stitched Materials Right here, we're looking at Alexandra Debler. She used CLO to design and develop her senior thesis collection inspired by the occult and tarot cards. Here's an example of the intricate beading design she developed in CLO, depicting the phases of the moon on the back of the jacket. Alex found a very clever way to use the animation feature in CLO, playing it back and then freezing the animation when she found the appropriate movement of the cloth that she wanted to use. Then she would do her final rendering. This is a render for a still image this way, showing the model in mid-stride. You can see that the fabric is floating in this image, with multi-layer fabric and the outer layer being chiffon or a sheer material. You can also see the radiant sunburst attachments that she made with sequins. The dress itself is actually one of her paintings that she turned into a print and put into a repeat for this dress. Another senior, Susima, patterned her entire collection on CLO and printed the patterns on her plotter to make twalls and her final garments. ### Advancements in 3D Body Measurement Students were also introduced to Trudiform, which is a 3D body measurement software that allows users to scan their models using their iPhones. After the scan, they were able to print the patterns with a simple pen. The model was printed before the scan, and after the scan is completed, the user receives an accurate measurement via an app. This can then be transferred into a CLO avatar. Along with this, they receive a 3D model in an OBJ format, along with all the measurements from their scanned model. I don't know if you've had the pleasure to meet Jim Simon in the New York CLO office, but he and I worked together to take this 3D scan of the model and then turn it into a CLO avatar. It worked out wonderfully. With her model scanned and now a CLO avatar, she could easily develop her designs and patterns with the correct fit for prototyping. This saved her a lot of time. ### CLO as a Design Tool Alyssa Boardman highlighted the benefits of using CLO in her CFDA scholarship application, stating that the use of a virtual 3D modeling software such as CLO 3D significantly reduces the cost and the use of materials to draft and design a collection. Alyssa also designed and printed her own textiles with the help of CLO. This collection was developed in conjunction with her junior tailoring studio. Using the edit texture tool, Alyssa could easily design and print her own textiles. This tool has been used to easily plan the most dynamic layout and scale of her print within her pattern pieces, providing her with a lot of flexibility. Here is the front and back view of her final render for her tailored jacket. ## Additional Projects and Innovations I use CLO as a primary design tool for my students to design various garments, including a customer outside the class. In addition to plants, we explore a mix of different types of waste pouring, so my students create designs that do not require pouring. The final Artemis capsule collection that they designed utilized the Oculus Quest VR to import their CLO models and Gravity Sketch, another program used for 3D modeling. This is where students created some environments for their final presentation. ### NASA's Artemis Mission A little bit about the class: NASA's Artemis Luna mission aims to return U.S. astronauts to the moon for the first time since 1972. The students were briefed to design an in-ship gender-neutral wardrobe for astronauts that would be functional, comfortable, sustainable, breathable, aesthetically pleasing, and easy to clean while being able to endure a mission to the moon. One of our students, Aventica, drew inspiration for her color story from the Aurora Borealis and found an iridescent fabric that was perfect for this in CLO Connect. For her capsule collection, Aventica, an ID student, incorporated ribbed joints for increased mobility, fabric loops in critical areas to hook sensors onto the garment, and hems that doubled as pockets—features that are very functional in a microgravity system. ### Student Work and Creative Exploration Alex, whose work we saw earlier, first learned CLO in "Pack Your Bags." She was a junior at the time. Her final renders for her Artemis collection focused on comfort, using a lot of cut-and-sew knit fabrics and playing with soft pastel colors, as well as a pop of red. We can see and appreciate her signature rendering technique. She also imported an HDRI file of a galaxy to use as the background for her CLO render. ### Fashion Revolution Workshop This fashion revolution, creating digital fashion for the Metaverse, was a class that I wrote and taught. It was a one-week workshop that I taught to middle and high school students in Shanghai and Beijing in the summer of 2023. CLO was the main design tool for the students to create their own avatars for the Metaverse, and they learned all about the Metaverse as well. The students were also introduced to AI text-to-image apps to help inspire their designs. I took the liberty of putting the students' names along with their ages on the artwork that we're looking at here. Interestingly, the younger students, ages 11, 12, and 13, picked up the program faster than the 15- to 18-year-olds. Given the one-week timeframe, I allowed students to download free CLO garments from the CLO Connect store as a starting point to then make their own designs and manipulations. They used the Edit Style Line tool to make adjustments, as well as the modular library and the 3D pen tools to develop their designs. At the age of 13, Gary got creative with the internal line tool to reshape his garments and had fun with the novelty fabrics he downloaded from CLO Connect. I was impressed with the students' outcomes and their abilities to navigate and use CLO all in the course of one week. ### Collaboration with NASA Michael Lai, the RISD NASA coordinator, designed and made this analog MS-1 Mars prototype spacesuit. In 2019, he asked me to pattern his spacesuit in CLO so we could make a few more prototypes for testing in a new design. We used the CLO patterns as a starting point for a new design for a spacesuit, and we did this in the summer of 2023. Last summer, in 2024, we formed a new company called XS3, which NASA has contracted us to make simulation spacesuits of their XEMU suits. This is what the suit looked like in pattern pieces; I haven't counted how many pattern pieces there are, but there are definitely a few hundred. This work inspired me to propose a class as a RISD elective called "NASA Spacesuits Reimagined and Redesigned," which I'm currently teaching right now. The motivation for both the chair that you see, which is a self-shaping textile, and the shoe, which is a 3D woven textile, was really to push what a textile could be.
